title: YouTube as a source of misinformation on COVID-19 vaccination: a systematic analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 150 most-viewed YouTube videos for the keyword 'COVID-19 vaccine' (searched 21 July 2021), 122 included. Two independent reviewers coded videos factual/non-factual against WHO and CDC guidance. Reports both the share of videos that were non-factual (13/122, 10.7%) and their share of total viewership (18,482,373/169,446,382, 11.0%). The mDISCERN/mJAMA/CVS quality scores are reported only as group means, never as shares for the whole sample, so they get no QUALITY row.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers (EP and OB-L) categorised every video in duplicate as factual or non-factual against WHO/CDC guidance, with a third reviewer (HO-YL) consulted for consensus. No inter-rater reliability statistic (kappa or percent agreement) is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: A YouTube search was performed on 21 July 2021, using keywords 'COVID-19 vaccine' on a cleared-cache web browser. Search results were sorted by 'views', and 150 videos with the greatest number of views were collected and analysed.
estimates.notes: Rank-truncated denominator (top 150 by views), hence denom_selection=curated: this is the prevalence among the most-viewed videos, not among all COVID-19 vaccine videos on YouTube. The video-level label is lenient in one direction (a single non-factual statement anywhere in the video flags the whole video) and strict in another (14 videos discussing none of the five CVS criteria were dropped rather than counted as factual). Authors note the figure is lower than the 27.5% and 45% reported by earlier studies and attribute this to YouTube's May 2020 COVID-19 medical misinformation policy.

estimates.notes: View-weighted counterpart of the 10.7% video-weighted row: same 122 videos, denominator is cumulative YouTube view counts rather than videos, so DENOMINATOR-sets-construct makes it EXPOSURE. borderline=true because these are platform-reported cumulative view counts for a curated top-150 set, not the news diet of any measured audience, and a view is not a person (repeat views and non-human views are included). The near-identity of the two figures (10.7% vs 11.0%) means non-factual videos were viewed at about the average rate: 'no significant differences in views per video (p=0.94)'.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) No QUALITY row. mDISCERN, mJAMA and the COVID-19 Vaccine Score are reported only as means split by source category (Table 1) or by factual/non-factual group (Table 2: mDISCERN 1.769 vs 3.651; mJAMA 0.538 vs 1.183; CVS 0.7 vs 0.948), never as a whole-sample mean and never as a share of videos above a threshold, so there is no extractable value. 2) '27.5% of the most viewed YouTube videos on COVID-19 contained misinformation' and the '45%' figure in the Discussion are cited from other studies (refs 11 and 16), which R8 forbids keeping. 3) Within-misinformation breakdowns not extracted: the source mix of the 13 non-factual videos (network news 4, healthcare professionals 3, education 2, internet news 2, newspaper 1, consumer 1), Table 3's counts of videos contradicting each reference standard (serious disease 1, vaccine effective 3, vaccine safe 6, contraindications 3), and '2 of the 13 videos (15.4%) containing non-factual information did not contain a YouTube information icon'. 4) Per-source prevalence could be assembled from Table 2's factual/non-factual category counts (e.g. internet news 2 non-factual and 4 factual), but building each denominator requires summing two cells, so no rows were created. 5) Engagement statistics (median likes/dislikes 13.89 for non-factual vs 2.33 for factual, p=0.00078; government videos 3.1 dislikes per like; entertainment 14.4 likes per dislike) and share of views by source category (health professionals 24.1%, network news 20.9%, education 16.9%, internet news 10.2%, consumers 8.4%, entertainment 8.1%, government 7.3%, newspapers 4.2%) are not misinformation shares. 6) '58.3% of Americans are fully vaccinated' is a vaccination statistic cited from the CDC. QUOTE FORM: the text file is a -layout rendering of a multi-column print page, so the printed sentences are interleaved with the neighbouring columns and no full sentence is contiguous in the file; each source_quote is therefore the exact within-line column fragment carrying the value, and the full sentence is reproduced in value_raw / measure_type.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Single YouTube search on 21 July 2021 for 'COVID-19 vaccine' from a cleared-cache browser, results sorted by views, top 150 taken; 28 excluded (14 discussing none of the five CVS criteria, 13 non-English, 1 non-audio), leaving 122. Three reviewers screened; two independent reviewers coded each video factual/non-factual and by publishing category in duplicate, with a third reviewer consulted for consensus, but NO inter-rater reliability statistic is reported. Reference standard: WHO and CDC guidance current at the time of each video's publication. Quality instruments were mDISCERN, mJAMA and a novel five-point COVID-19 Vaccine Score adapted from prior work. Analysis by two-tailed t-tests and Mann-Whitney U with a p<0.01 threshold. No country restriction is stated and no attempt was made to account for search personalisation beyond clearing the cache; a single search on a single day means the sampling frame is one snapshot of YouTube's ranking. No funding declared, no competing interests, ethics approval not required, and the authors state no dataset is available for sharing.
rob.item6_quote: Videos were considered non-factual if they contained one or more non-factual statements, defined as contradictory to guidelines published by public health agencies (ie, WHO or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) at the time of video publication.
rob.item10_quote: Thirteen videos (10.7%) contained non-factual information and accounted for 11.0% of total viewership, while 109 videos (89.3%) contained only factual information.
